Sound is a key signal through which vocal vertebrates interact with their environment. These animals pick up information from the sounds around them, and they also produce sounds that act on their surroundings. From simple single syllables to combinations of complex ones, the evolution of vocal systems is the evolutionary history of how animals pass information to one another. Species that can command more complex sounds undoubtedly gain a head start in survival and reproduction.

Since sound carries such important information, some individuals are bound to exploit it for their own gain. Let us start with kouji, the traditional Chinese art of vocal mimicry in which a performer imitates every sound under heaven, move on to vocal mimicry in birds, and take a look at the biology behind both skills.

1. Kouji: the human mimic

Suddenly a hundred, a thousand people were shouting; a hundred, a thousand children wailing; a hundred, a thousand dogs barking. Through it all came the crack and crash of falling timbers, the roar of the flames, the howl of the wind, a hundred, a thousand sounds at once; and mixed among them, a hundred, a thousand cries for help, the heave-ho of men dragging down the house, the scramble to save belongings, the splash of water. Every sound that ought to be there was there.

Then the clapper struck the table once, and every sound was gone. The screen was drawn back, and there was one man, one table, one chair, one fan, one clapper, nothing more.

— Excerpt from “The Mimic” (Kouji) by Lin Sihuan, Qing dynasty

Figure 1. A storyteller (AI-generated)

“The Mimic,” a classical prose piece that generations of Chinese students have read at school, vividly portrays a performance by a folk artist of uncanny skill. With nothing but his mouth, the performer not only produces a wide range of convincingly real sounds but weaves them together, so that a complete scene unfolds before the audience, layered and building step by step: the stillness of a deep alley at night; a family of four drifting from sleep to waking and back to sleep; and finally the panic and stampede when fire breaks out. The piece captures to perfection the magic of the art and the performer’s power to conjure “every sound that ought to be there” from “one man, one table, one chair, one fan, one clapper.” It shows the consummate skill of folk artists in building a lifelike soundscape through imitation alone. And this voice, which can imitate everything and paint whole scenes in sound, comes from an organ that humans share with most mammals: the vocal folds.

2. The vocal folds

The vocal folds (often called vocal cords) sit at the top of the trachea, in the larynx: a pair of elastic folds that act as a biological reed. These reeds work like a pair of smart, folding double doors. Most of the time the doors stand open to let air through (breathing); when needed, they vibrate to make sound (speaking); and at the critical moment of swallowing they snap tightly shut, working with a second door further up, the epiglottis, as a double safeguard that keeps food from going down the wrong way. When we speak, shout or even cough, a controlled stream of air from the lungs forces its way through the closed reeds and sets them vibrating, and a raw sound is born. This raw sound is then amplified and colored by the resonating cavities of the throat, mouth and nose, sculpted by the tongue, lips, teeth and palate, and supported by gesture and movement. Under the control of the nervous system, with many systems and organs working together, the journey runs from the first raw sound, to the performance of complex sounds, to the lifelike imitation of every sound in creation, and an exquisite feast of sound unfolds before the audience.

Figure 2. Location of the human vocal folds (image from the internet)

3. Mimicry: the bird’s kouji

A short, slightly hoarse call: I thought a red-billed blue magpie had turned up in our housing estate, but it was a Chinese blackbird. A sweet, warbling song: I followed it, expecting a light-vented bulbul, and found another blackbird. These were a few of the blunders I made when I first took up birdwatching. Only later did I learn that some birds are skilled at kouji too, an ability known as vocal mimicry. Vocal mimicry is the behavior of certain birds that imitate the calls of other birds, other animals or environmental noise; in plain terms, birds copying the sounds around them.

Figure 3. Chinese blackbird (top panel from lecture slides by Zhongqiu Li)

The Chinese blackbird (Turdus mandarinus) is widespread across central and eastern China and neighboring regions and is a common city bird. In my housing estate I am as likely to meet one as a spotted dove or a light-vented bulbul. Because it is such a gifted mimic, Chinese folk tradition calls it baishe, “hundred tongues”; for its endlessly varied song it is also hailed as the “king of songbirds,” and some people keep it as a cage bird. Not long ago, in an online lecture, Zhongqiu Li of Nanjing University said that his team had recorded more than a hundred mimicked calls from Chinese blackbirds, including an imitation of an electric scooter’s alarm. The source of these hundred-plus borrowed calls is an organ found only in birds: the syrinx.

4. The syrinx

4.1 The tracheobronchial syrinx

The human vocal folds sit at the top of the trachea; the bird’s syrinx lies at the very bottom, where the trachea divides into the two bronchi. Its structure varies widely among birds. Depending on how much the trachea and the bronchi contribute, syringes are usually classed as tracheal, bronchial or tracheobronchial. The most common and typical is the tracheobronchial syrinx, built from both tracheal and bronchial rings.

The tracheobronchial syrinx is formed from the last few tracheal rings at the bottom of the trachea and the first few rings of the two bronchi, enlarged and reshaped. (Both the trachea and the bronchi consist of cartilage rings with a tube wall covering them inside and out; picture a wire-reinforced PVC hose.) It is a three-way junction in the airway: the trachea is the main road and the two bronchi are the branches. Or picture an upside-down slingshot: the handle is the trachea, and the two prongs that hold the rubber band are the bronchi.

Figure 4. Location and structure of the syrinx (from “Decoding birdsong: a short introduction to bird vocalizations,” an original article by Pteryx Sun on the WeChat account Gu Niao Za Tan, 2023-10-16)

4.2 The syringeal membranes

Where the cartilage rings enlarge, the wall of the forked part of the syrinx thins and becomes a specialized biological membrane, the tympaniform membrane, which vibrates in the airflow to make sound. It works rather like the thin membrane stretched over a hole in a Chinese dizi flute: the airflow sets the membrane into fast, regular vibration and turns moving air into sound. But the syringeal membranes are finely controlled by the syringeal muscles attached to the syrinx, and helped by the expansion, contraction and resonance of the air sac that surrounds it, so the syrinx can produce far more varied pitches and timbres. In some birds the left and right halves of the syrinx can even be controlled independently, producing two different sounds at once.

More remarkable still, a bird’s syrinx can make sound both when it breathes in and when it breathes out, whereas our vocal folds sound only on the out-breath. Think of whistling: can’t you whistle both blowing out and drawing in? The physics is similar to the syrinx, though the syrinx is far more complex. Voicing on both the in-breath and the out-breath makes highly efficient use of the airflow, and this almost uninterrupted sound production lets birds perform longer, more fluid and more beautiful “melodies,” which sound all the more lilting to us. That is why the organ was named after Syrinx, the nymph of Greek myth who was turned into the reeds of Pan’s pipes.

5. A who’s who of mimics

5.1 Masters next door

Nature has many skilled mimics. Songbirds stand out, and there is no shortage of virtuosos among them. Besides the familiar Chinese blackbird, they include the crested myna and the pet parrot. A trained, caged crested myna can imitate simple human speech. Its family, the starlings and mynas (Sturnidae), is famous for varied calls, and its member the common hill myna is an outstanding “linguist” whose powers of imitation are second to none. Hill mynas imitate human voices and environmental sounds clearly and accurately, and they learn fast. People have observed hill mynas imitating a cough, a ringing telephone and a barking dog, and even teaching themselves to sing Peking opera. Compared with crested mynas, parrots and other vocal birds, hill mynas usually pronounce more clearly and smoothly.

Figure 5. Crested myna

Figure 6. The common hill myna (illustration from A Field Guide to the Birds of China by John MacKinnon)

5.2 Masters abroad

Birds that mimic usually borrow selectively, copying characteristic syllables or fragments from other birds’ calls or from environmental sounds. After all, the point is not to win an impressions contest through the highest possible fidelity. For many mimics, a few key fragments are enough to serve survival and reproduction. Some especially gifted master mimics, however, can blend and recombine syllables and fragments from different sources into a long, new and complex symphony, much as a DJ mixes the best-known bits of different songs into a brand-new medley. Which brings us to a bird that has also been called “the mother of songbirds”: the superb lyrebird.

The superb lyrebird is a songbird found only in Australia. I first met it in the BBC documentary Secret World of Sound with David Attenborough. In it, Attenborough says the lyrebird has “the most elaborate, most complex and most beautiful song in the world.” It is said that a lyrebird can imitate almost any sound it has heard, from the natural world or the human one; a single lyrebird can be a whole band, and anyone listening feels as if they were enjoying a beautiful, pure symphony.

Figure 7. Secret World of Sound with David Attenborough (still from the BBC documentary)

Figure 8. Superb lyrebird (still from Secret World of Sound with David Attenborough)

6. What mimicry is for

6.1 Attracting a mate

Vocal mimicry in birds may have begun as accidental learning errors, but it evolved into a powerful aid to survival and reproduction. Many researchers believe its core driver is sexual selection.

For many songbirds, whether a male wins a female’s favor depends on the richness of his song library, and that depends directly on how good a mimic he is. Mimicry is a complex learning process that requires listening, observing, memorizing, recalling and practicing again and again. It takes physical stamina as well as strong learning ability, cognitive ability and precise muscle control. Mimicry is therefore an important indicator of a bird’s cognitive ability and physical vigor, and a large, complex song library is the résumé a male presents to females. In a female’s eyes, the more complex and varied a male’s song, the smarter, healthier and more experienced he is, the better his genes and the higher his fitness, and so the more attractive he is.

6.2 Intimidation

Beyond courtship, mimicry also matters for survival. Complex, intimidating imitations can scare off competitors and predators, and can even be used to “scare up a meal,” frightening other animals off their food and taking it without effort. Male superb lyrebirds even imitate alarm calls after mating, so that the female freezes in vigilance and stays still; this prolongs copulation and raises the chances of fertilization.

6.3 Social life

Besides courtship and intimidation, mimicry is also vital to the social life of some group-living birds. For them, the group’s shared “dialect” is an identity card. By imitating and mastering the group’s particular calls, an individual can fit in more easily, join in group activities and avoid conflict, which keeps the peace. It is much like moving somewhere new to live or work: if you can speak the local dialect fluently, you will no doubt settle into the community faster, earn trust more easily and get your work done more smoothly.

7. A mimicry arms race

Vocal mimicry in birds is a product of convergent behavioral evolution: this complex behavior appears in many birds around the globe that are not closely related. The way mimicry evolves, and the way birds learn to imitate, is strikingly similar to how we learn a foreign language, English for instance. Our motivation to learn English comes from the selection pressure of surviving and thriving in a globalized world: better economic opportunities, better education and a stronger cultural voice. But the learner’s own aptitude for languages, the speech habits of their mother tongue and the level of their teacher (a native speaker, say, or someone who learned English secondhand) all affect the result. Hence the many regional varieties of English spoken around the world.

Molecular biology has revealed that songbird mimicry and human language learning do share part of their genetic basis. Some genes that play a key role in human language also matter in songbirds, such as the star gene of language research, FOXP2. Studies show that in birds that are skilled vocal imitators, FOXP2 is expressed in the brain in a pattern very similar to that in humans. Defects in FOXP2 impair brain development and neural plasticity in humans and cause language disorders. In songbirds, FOXP2 is a key regulator of song learning, responsible for imitating, learning and precisely correcting songs; when its function is impaired, adult songbirds show some symptoms resembling human language disorders.

Because of these similar learning mechanisms, birds of the same species develop their own song “dialects” in different places, while different species imitate different models. Together, this produces clear differences in singing ability between individuals of the same species.

In most birds, females are a relatively scarce resource, so every breeding season some males lose out and stay single. To win a mate, a male must keep honing his craft and expanding his repertoire. The better the mimic, the more competitive he is against other males; the fiercer the competition, the higher the bar for mimicry. An acoustic arms race becomes inevitable.

8. Voices in the forest

Look closely and you will find that most skilled mimics in nature are forest birds. In a forest, leaves and branches block the view and the light is dim, so recognizing a bird by its voice becomes the most effective way to communicate. Curiously, this mirrors some human cultural traditions. Many of China’s ethnic minorities who live deep in the mountains have a tradition of “song as matchmaker”: young men and women separated by hills and rivers sing folk songs back and forth to show off their talent, share their feelings and find a partner, much as a male bird in the woods sings the most complex song he can to win a female. Of course, for humans, singing is one craft among many, a matter of art and of life; for birds that depend on song to attract a mate, it is a compulsory course in survival on which the passing on of their genes depends.

Figure 9. Courtship in song (AI-generated image meant to evoke the mood; not a record of a real scene)

9. The law of nature and human ethics

In a forest, where leafy branches hide birds from one another, a listener can mistake one bird for another by its voice, and the mimic profits. In today’s society, aren’t scams that use imitated or synthesized voices built on the same trick, using a “familiar voice” to make people mistake who is speaking? The difference is that mimicry in wild animals follows nature’s law of natural selection and survival of the fittest, with no question of morality, law or empathy; an animal that is frightened away is simply avoiding danger by instinct. Voice scams, by contrast, exploit the moral code of honesty, kindness, trust and mutual help that each of us ought to live by. They damage the social contract that all of us should uphold to keep society stable. The harm they do far outweighs any “gain,” and a civilized society must firmly resist and punish them as the cancer they are.

10. A caveat and a recommendation

Finally, a caveat: this article draws many analogies with human behavior, mainly to help explain the evolutionary logic behind certain bird behaviors. Although humans are animals in biological classification, human imitation involves extremely complex psychological, emotional and sociocultural factors, so research on it usually belongs to psychology or sociology rather than zoology.

If bird mimicry interests you, I recommend Jennifer Ackerman’s book The Bird Way, which has a wealth of fascinating material on vocal mimicry.

Figure 10. Cover of The Bird Way

My knowledge is limited, so corrections and additions are very welcome.

Note: This article first appeared on Xiaopeng Huo’s blog at ScienceNet.cn on September 16, 2025, and has been slightly revised.

About the author: Xiaopeng Huo is a member of the China Science Writers Association. Since completing his master’s degree in 2009, he has worked in ecology, and in his spare time he writes popular science about nature.
